kangaroo-at-2015-student-01.title: Extreme cases
kangaroo-at-2015-student-01.body:
The age difference is smallest if Andrea was born on 31 December 1997 and Charlotte on 1 January 2001: just over **3 years**. It is largest if Andrea was born on 1 January 1997 and Charlotte on 31 December 2001: almost **5 years**.

So the difference can be less than 4, equal to 4 or more than 4 years; (A)–(D) are all not certain. But it is always more than 3 years, i.e. not less than 3 years.

**Answer: (E) not less than 3 years**

kangaroo-at-2015-student-01.title: Rule out options
kangaroo-at-2015-student-01.body:
- 31 Dec 1997 and 1 Jan 2001 give about 3 years: this rules out (B), (C) and (D).
- 1 Jan 1997 and 31 Dec 2001 give almost 5 years: this rules out (A).

Only (E) survives, and it is always true because the dates are more than three full years apart.

**Answer: (E) not less than 3 years**

kangaroo-at-2015-student-02.title: Opposite numbers
kangaroo-at-2015-student-02.body:
$b - a = -(a - b)$, so $(b-a)^3 = -(a-b)^3$ (an odd power keeps the sign). The two terms cancel: the sum is $0$.

**Answer: (A) 0**

kangaroo-at-2015-student-03.title: Same base
kangaroo-at-2015-student-03.body:
$2^{2x} = (2^2)^x = 4^x$. The equation becomes $4^x = 4^{x+1} = 4 \cdot 4^x$, i.e. $3 \cdot 4^x = 0$. Since $4^x > 0$ for all real $x$, there is no solution.

**Answer: (A) 0**

kangaroo-at-2015-student-03.title: Compare exponents
kangaroo-at-2015-student-03.body:
Write both sides as powers of 2: $2^{2x} = 2^{2x+2}$. Powers of 2 are equal only when the exponents are equal: $2x = 2x + 2$, which is impossible.

**Answer: (A) 0**

kangaroo-at-2015-student-04.title: Read off the proportions
kangaroo-at-2015-student-04.body:
Measure the bars: light grey $\approx 4$ units, black $\approx 1$, white $\approx 3$, dark grey $\approx 2$ (total 10). So the pie chart needs light grey $\approx 40\%$ (a bit less than half the circle), white $\approx 30\%$, dark grey $\approx 20\%$ and black $\approx 10\%$ (the smallest sector).

Chart (A) has exactly this: light grey a bit less than half, white a bit less than a third, dark grey about a fifth, black the smallest slice.

**Answer: (A)**

kangaroo-at-2015-student-04.title: Eliminate
kangaroo-at-2015-student-04.body:
- (C) and (D): light grey is not the largest sector, but it is the tallest bar.
- (E): light grey is far more than half; its bar is less than half of the total.
- (B): the white sector is about as big as the light grey one, and black is almost as big as dark grey; the bars show white clearly smaller than light grey and black only half of dark grey.

Only (A) remains.

**Answer: (A)**

kangaroo-at-2015-student-05.title: Average
kangaroo-at-2015-student-05.body:
There are $2031 - 2001 + 1 = 31$ numbers, so dividing their sum by 31 gives their average. For consecutive numbers the average is the middle one: $\frac{2001 + 2031}{2} = 2016$.

**Answer: (D) 2016**

kangaroo-at-2015-student-06.title: Count odd points (Euler)
kangaroo-at-2015-student-06.body:
A figure can be drawn in one stroke exactly when it is connected and has $0$ or $2$ points where an odd number of lines meet.

1. Circle with a line through it: two crossing points (4 lines each) and two free ends (1 each) → 2 odd points. **Yes.**
2. Circle with two line pieces touching it from outside: the two touching points have 3 lines, plus 2 free ends → 4 odd points. **No.**
3. Two circles with a line through them: 4 crossing points (even), 2 free ends → 2 odd points. **Yes.**
4. Three circles with a line: 6 crossing points (even), 2 free ends → **Yes.**

So 3 shapes can be drawn.

**Answer: (D) 3**

kangaroo-at-2015-student-06.title: Draw them
kangaroo-at-2015-student-06.body:
For figure 1: start at the left end, go along the line to the circle, travel around the whole circle back to the same point, and continue along the line to the right end. Figures 3 and 4 work the same way: each time you reach a circle, go once around it and then continue along the line.

In figure 2, the line pieces end on the circle: once you arrive at the circle from the left you can go around one half of the circle to the right piece, but the other half of the circle is then left over and cannot be added without retracing.

**Answer: (D) 3**

kangaroo-at-2015-student-07.title: Angle sum
kangaroo-at-2015-student-07.body:
The angles of a quadrilateral add up to $360^\circ$. If three angles are right angles, the fourth is $360^\circ - 270^\circ = 90^\circ$, so it is right too: $n = 3$ is impossible.

All other values occur: a rhombus that is not a square has $n = 0$; the quadrilateral with vertices $(0,0), (3,0), (2,3), (0,1)$ has only the right angle at the origin, $n = 1$; a right trapezoid such as $(0,0), (3,0), (2,2), (0,2)$ has $n = 2$; a rectangle has $n = 4$.

**Answer: (B) 0, 1, 2, 4**

kangaroo-at-2015-student-07.title: Eliminate
kangaroo-at-2015-student-07.body:
A rectangle has 4 right angles, so the list must contain 4: only (B) and (C) remain. Three right angles force the fourth angle to be $90^\circ$, so 3 is not possible, which rules out (C).

**Answer: (B) 0, 1, 2, 4**

kangaroo-at-2015-student-08.title: Unroll the cone
kangaroo-at-2015-student-08.body:
The side of a full cone unrolls into a circular sector (the apex becomes the centre, the base circle becomes the arc). A truncated cone is a big cone with a small cone cut off at the top, so its side unrolls into a big sector with a smaller sector (same centre and angle) removed: a part of a ring bounded by two concentric arcs and two radii. That is shape (E).

**Answer: (E)**

kangaroo-at-2015-student-08.title: Eliminate shapes
kangaroo-at-2015-student-08.body:
The top and bottom edges of the glass are circles of different sizes, so on the paper they must become curved edges of different lengths. (A) and (B) have straight top and bottom edges; (C) has only one arc; (D) has two arcs but they bend in opposite directions/are not parts of concentric circles. Only (E) has two concentric arcs joined by straight segments that point to the common centre.

**Answer: (E)**

kangaroo-at-2015-student-09.title: Pythagoras
kangaroo-at-2015-student-09.body:
A semicircle on a side of length $s$ has area $\frac{\pi}{8}s^2$. With legs $p$, $q$ and hypotenuse $r$ we have $p^2 + q^2 = r^2$; multiplying by $\frac{\pi}{8}$ gives $X + Y = Z$.

**Answer: (C) $X + Y = Z$**

kangaroo-at-2015-student-09.title: Example
kangaroo-at-2015-student-09.body:
Take the 3-4-5 triangle: $X = \frac{9\pi}{8}$, $Y = \frac{16\pi}{8}$, $Z = \frac{25\pi}{8}$. Then $X + Y = Z$ holds, while (A), (B), (D), (E) fail.

**Answer: (C) $X + Y = Z$**

kangaroo-at-2015-student-10.title: Track the grid points
kangaroo-at-2015-student-10.body:
Put coordinates $0, 1, 2, 3$ on the grid lines in each direction. Folding along all dashed lines (in any order and direction) stacks the 9 small squares; a point with coordinate $x$ lands on $0$ if $x$ is even and on $1$ if $x$ is odd (folds reflect, so the coordinate's parity is what matters). The same holds for $y$.

A corner of the folded small square has coordinates $(a, b)$ with $a, b \in \{0, 1\}$; cutting it cuts all grid points $(x, y)$ with $x \equiv a$, $y \equiv b \pmod 2$. Holes appear only at the 4 interior grid points $(1,1), (1,2), (2,1), (2,2)$ — and exactly one of them has each parity pattern. Cuts at other grid points are on the edge (notches) or at a corner, not holes.

So there is exactly **1** hole (a small diamond around one crossing point of the dashed lines); all other cuts are notches on the border.

**Answer: (B) 1**

kangaroo-at-2015-student-12.title: Euler's formula
kangaroo-at-2015-student-12.body:
Intersection points:
- $f$ with the $x$-axis: $x = \pm\sqrt2$; $g$ with the $x$-axis: $x = \pm 1$;
- $f = g$: $2 - x^2 = x^2 - 1$, $x = \pm\sqrt{3/2}$ (at $y = \tfrac12$, not on the axis).

So there are 6 distinct points, and each curve carries 4 of them, cutting it into 5 pieces: $E = 15$ edges. Add one point "at infinity" where all unbounded pieces meet: $V = 7$. Euler's formula $V - E + F = 2$ gives $F = 2 - 7 + 15 = 10$ regions.

**Answer: (D) 10 regions**

kangaroo-at-2015-student-12.title: Add curves one by one
kangaroo-at-2015-student-12.body:
The $x$-axis alone gives 2 regions. A new curve that crosses existing curves in $k$ points (and goes off to infinity at both ends) adds $k + 1$ regions.
- $g$ crosses the axis twice: $+3$, total 5.
- $f$ crosses the axis twice and $g$ twice: $+5$, total 10.

**Answer: (D) 10 regions**

kangaroo-at-2015-student-13.title: Period of the sequence
kangaroo-at-2015-student-13.body:
Go round the circle and call the numbers $a_1, a_2, \dots, a_8$. The condition $a_i = a_{i-1} + a_{i+1}$ gives $a_{i+1} = a_i - a_{i-1}$. Starting from $x, y$ the sequence is
$$x,\ y,\ y-x,\ -x,\ -y,\ x-y,\ x,\ y, \dots$$
so it repeats every 6 steps and $a_{i+3} = -a_i$.

There are 8 circles, so also $a_{i+8} = a_i$. Together with period 6 this gives $a_{i+2} = a_i$. Then $a_i = a_{i-1} + a_{i+1} = 2a_{i+1}$ and likewise $a_{i+1} = 2a_i$, so $a_i = 4a_i$, i.e. all numbers are $0$. But the circles already contain 3 and 5, so Ella cannot do it.

**Answer: (E) This question has no solution.**

kangaroo-at-2015-student-13.title: Opposite numbers
kangaroo-at-2015-student-13.body:
From $a_{i+3} = -a_i$ (shown above): $a_1 = -a_4 = a_7 = -a_{10} = -a_2$ (indices mod 8), and the same way $a_2 = -a_3$, $a_3 = -a_4$, … so neighbours are always opposite numbers: $a_{i+1} = -a_i$. Then $a_i = a_{i-1} + a_{i+1} = -a_i - a_i = -2a_i$, so $a_i = 0$ for all $i$. But two circles already contain 3 and 5. Impossible.

**Answer: (E) This question has no solution.**

kangaroo-at-2015-student-14.title: Chain of inequalities
kangaroo-at-2015-student-14.body:
- $d = a + b$ gives $d > a$ and $d > b$.
- $a = e - d$ gives $e = a + d > d$.
- $b = c : e$ gives $c = b \cdot e$. Since $b$ is a positive whole number different from... if $b = 1$ then $c = e$, which is not allowed; so $b \ge 2$ and $c = be > e$.

Hence $c > e > d > a, b$.

**Answer: (C) $c$**

kangaroo-at-2015-student-14.title: Example
kangaroo-at-2015-student-14.body:
Try $a = 1$, $b = 2$: $d = 3$, $e = a + d = 4$, $c = b e = 8$. The numbers $1, 2, 8, 3, 4$ are all different and $c = 8$ is the largest. The inequalities above show this always happens.

**Answer: (C) $c$**

kangaroo-at-2015-student-15.title: Products
kangaroo-at-2015-student-15.body:
The first three numbers have product $3^3 = 27$, the other three $12^3 = 1728$. All six have product $27 \cdot 1728 = (3 \cdot 12)^3 = 36^3$. The geometric mean is $\sqrt[6]{36^3} = \sqrt{36} = 6$.

**Answer: (B) 6**

kangaroo-at-2015-student-15.title: Mean of the means
kangaroo-at-2015-student-15.body:
The geometric mean of two equal-sized groups is the geometric mean of the two group means: $\sqrt{3 \cdot 12} = \sqrt{36} = 6$. (Check with $3,3,3,12,12,12$.)

**Answer: (B) 6**

kangaroo-at-2015-student-16.title: Quarter areas
kangaroo-at-2015-student-16.body:
Let the radii be $1 < r < R$. The grey parts are a quarter of the small disc, a quarter of the middle ring and a quarter of the outer ring:
$$\tfrac{\pi}{4}\cdot 1 = \tfrac{\pi}{4}(r^2 - 1) = \tfrac{\pi}{4}(R^2 - r^2).$$
So $r^2 = 2$ and $R^2 = 3$. The product is $1 \cdot \sqrt2 \cdot \sqrt3 = \sqrt6$.

**Answer: (A) $\sqrt6$**

kangaroo-at-2015-student-16.title: Equal steps of area
kangaroo-at-2015-student-16.body:
Equal grey quarters mean the three discs have areas in ratio $1 : 2 : 3$ (each ring adds as much as the first disc). Areas scale with the square of the radius, so the radii are $1, \sqrt2, \sqrt3$ with product $\sqrt6$.

**Answer: (A) $\sqrt6$**

kangaroo-at-2015-student-17.title: Equation
kangaroo-at-2015-student-17.body:
Let the old populations be $a$ and $b$. Then $1.4a + 1.6b = 1.54(a + b)$, so $0.06b = 0.14a$, i.e. $a : b = 0.06 : 0.14 = 3 : 7$.

**Answer: (C) 3:7**

kangaroo-at-2015-student-17.title: Weighted average
kangaroo-at-2015-student-17.body:
The total growth $54\%$ is a weighted average of $40\%$ and $60\%$. It is $14$ points above $40$ and $6$ points below $60$, so the weights are in ratio $6 : 14 = 3 : 7$ (the village closer to the average, Berghausen, is the bigger one).

**Answer: (C) 3:7**

kangaroo-at-2015-student-18.title: Two cases
kangaroo-at-2015-student-18.body:
- Tina rolls 2 (probability $\frac12$): she wins if Bibi rolls 1, probability $\frac16$.
- Tina rolls 5 (probability $\frac12$): she wins if Bibi rolls 1–4, probability $\frac46$.

$P = \frac12\cdot\frac16 + \frac12\cdot\frac46 = \frac{5}{12}$.

**Answer: (C) $\frac{5}{12}$**

kangaroo-at-2015-student-18.title: Count outcomes
kangaroo-at-2015-student-18.body:
Of the $6 \cdot 6 = 36$ equally likely pairs, Tina's three 2-faces beat 1 face of Bibi ($3$ pairs) and her three 5-faces beat 4 faces ($12$ pairs). $\frac{15}{36} = \frac{5}{12}$.

**Answer: (C) $\frac{5}{12}$**

kangaroo-at-2015-student-19.title: Range of digit sums
kangaroo-at-2015-student-19.body:
The number of colours is the number of different digit sums. The smallest is $1$ (marble 1); the largest is $1 + 9 + 9 + 9 = 28$ (marble 1999). Every value in between occurs, e.g. $1, \dots, 9$ from one-digit numbers, $10, \dots, 18$ from $19, 29, \dots, 99$, $19, \dots, 27$ from $199, 299, \dots, 999$, and $28$ from $1999$. So there are 28 colours.

**Answer: (C) 28**

kangaroo-at-2015-student-19.title: Check the top
kangaroo-at-2015-student-19.body:
No number up to 2015 has digit sum 29 or more: four-digit numbers here start with 1 or 2, and those starting with 2 are at most $2015$ (digit sum $\le 8$); those starting with 1 have digit sum at most $1 + 27 = 28$. All sums 1–28 are reached, giving 28 colours.

**Answer: (C) 28**

kangaroo-at-2015-student-20.title: Rotate the left die
kangaroo-at-2015-student-20.body:
The left die shows front 1, top 2, left 3; so back 6, bottom 5, right 4. The right die shows top 6 and front 4. Since the dice are identical, turn the left die into this position:
1. Tip it backwards so the back face comes to the top: now top 6, front 2, bottom 1, back 5, left 3, right 4.
2. Turn it about the vertical axis so the right face comes to the front: now front 4, left 2, back 3, right **5** (top still 6).

So the hidden right face of the right die shows 5.

**Answer: (A) only 5**

kangaroo-at-2015-student-20.title: Orientation of a corner
kangaroo-at-2015-student-20.body:
Around a corner of a die the three faces appear in a fixed rotational order. On the left die, the front–top–right corner has faces $1, 2, 4$ in that order (clockwise when looking at the corner). Replacing one face by its opposite reverses the order. On the right die the front–top–right corner has $4, 6, ?$. From $(1,2,4)$ replace $1 \to 6$ (reversed) and $2 \to 5$ (reversed again): $(6, 5, 4)$ has the same order as $(1, 2, 4)$, and so does its rotation $(4, 6, 5)$. So $? = 5$; the value 2 would give the mirror-image die.

**Answer: (A) only 5**

kangaroo-at-2015-student-21.title: Work from the end
kangaroo-at-2015-student-21.body:
- (E) $1 + 1 = 2$ is true.
- So (C) "(E) is false" is false.
- So (A) "(C) is true" is false.
- So (B) "(A) is true" is false.
- So (D) "(B) is false" is true.

The true statements are (D) and (E); the first one is (D).

**Answer: (D)**

kangaroo-at-2015-student-21.title: Test the earlier ones
kangaroo-at-2015-student-21.body:
If (A) were true, (C) would be true, so (E) would be false — but $1+1=2$. So (A) is false, hence (B) is false too, and (C) is false because (E) is true. (D) says (B) is false, which is correct, so (D) is the first true statement.

**Answer: (D)**

kangaroo-at-2015-student-22.title: Symmetry and the origin
kangaroo-at-2015-student-22.body:
The origin satisfies the equation ($0 = 0$), so it is the point where the curve crosses itself — the common point of all four lines. Replacing $y$ by $-y$ does not change the equation, so the curve is symmetric about the $x$-axis. In the picture the only symmetry axis of the curve is line $c$ (it runs through the small loop and the middle of the big loop). So $c$ is the $x$-axis and the $y$-axis is the line through the origin perpendicular to $c$: line $a$.

**Answer: (A) $a$**

kangaroo-at-2015-student-22.title: Polar form
kangaroo-at-2015-student-22.body:
With $x = r\cos\theta$, $y = r\sin\theta$: $(r^2 - 2r\cos\theta)^2 = 2r^2$, so $r = 2\cos\theta \pm \sqrt2$. The big loop ($r = 2\cos\theta + \sqrt2$) reaches farthest, $r = 2 + \sqrt2$, at $\theta = 0$, i.e. along the positive $x$-axis; the small loop also lies on the positive $x$-axis ($r = 2 - \sqrt2$). Both lie along line $c$, so $c$ is the $x$-axis, and the $y$-axis is the perpendicular line $a$. (Also: $r = 0$ at $\cos\theta = \pm\frac{1}{\sqrt2}$, so the curve's tangents at the origin are at $45^\circ$ to the axes — lines $b$ and $d$.)

**Answer: (A) $a$**

kangaroo-at-2015-student-23.title: Row by row
kangaroo-at-2015-student-23.body:
Row $i$ is $i, 2i, \dots, 10i$ with sum $55i$. Adding the rows: $55(1 + 2 + \dots + 10) = 55 \cdot 55 = 3025$.

**Answer: (D) 3025**

kangaroo-at-2015-student-24.title: Exterior angles
kangaroo-at-2015-student-24.body:
The interior angle of a regular $n$-gon is $180^\circ - \frac{360^\circ}{n}$. It is a whole number exactly when $n$ divides $360 = 2^3\cdot 3^2 \cdot 5$. 360 has $4 \cdot 3 \cdot 2 = 24$ divisors; removing $n = 1$ and $n = 2$ (no polygon) leaves 22.

**Answer: (C) 22**

kangaroo-at-2015-student-25.title: Binary digits
kangaroo-at-2015-student-25.body:
A sum of different powers of two is a binary representation, so we need three-digit numbers with exactly nine 1s in binary. Since $2^{10} = 1024 > 999$, at most 10 binary digits are used.
- Nine digits, all 1: $2^9 - 1 = 511$.
- Ten digits with exactly one 0: $1023 - 2^k$ for $k = 0, \dots, 8$: $1022, 1021, 1019, 1015, 1007, 991, 959, 895, 767$. Of these, $991, 959, 895, 767$ are below 1000.

Total: $1 + 4 = 5$.

**Answer: (E) 5**

kangaroo-at-2015-student-25.title: From the top
kangaroo-at-2015-student-25.body:
The smallest sum of nine different powers of two is $1 + 2 + \dots + 2^8 = 511$, already three digits. Any other choice must include $2^9 = 512$ and drop one of $2^0, \dots, 2^8$ (using $2^{10}$ or more exceeds 999). Dropping $2^k$ gives $1023 - 2^k \le 999$ iff $2^k \ge 24$, i.e. $k = 5, 6, 7, 8$. Together with 511: 5 numbers.

**Answer: (E) 5**

kangaroo-at-2015-student-26.title: Difference of squares
kangaroo-at-2015-student-26.body:
$AB = 20$ is a leg; let the other leg be $a$ and the hypotenuse $c$. Then $c^2 - a^2 = 400$, i.e. $(c - a)(c + a) = 400$. Both factors have the same parity, so both are even: $c - a = 2u$, $c + a = 2v$ with $uv = 100$, $u < v$. The pairs $(u, v)$ are $(1,100), (2,50), (4,25), (5,20)$, giving $a = v - u = 99, 48, 21, 15$ and $c = 101, 52, 29, 25$. So there are 4 triangles.

**Answer: (D) 4**

kangaroo-at-2015-student-26.title: Pythagorean triples
kangaroo-at-2015-student-26.body:
Triples with a leg of 20: $(20, 99, 101)$ (primitive), $(20, 21, 29)$ (primitive), $(15, 20, 25) = 5\cdot(3,4,5)$, $(20, 48, 52) = 4\cdot(5,12,13)$. The factorisation argument shows there are no others.

**Answer: (D) 4**

kangaroo-at-2015-student-27.title: Coordinates
kangaroo-at-2015-student-27.body:
Ratios of areas don't change under stretching, so take $A = (0,0)$, $B = (1,0)$, $C = (1,1)$, $D = (0,1)$. Then
$M_1 = (\tfrac12, 1)$, $M_2 = (\tfrac14, \tfrac12)$, $M_3 = (\tfrac58, \tfrac14)$, $M_4 = (\tfrac{13}{16}, \tfrac58)$.

Shoelace: $2\cdot\text{Area} = \left|(\tfrac12\cdot\tfrac12 - \tfrac14\cdot 1) + (\tfrac14\cdot\tfrac14 - \tfrac58\cdot\tfrac12) + (\tfrac58\cdot\tfrac58 - \tfrac{13}{16}\cdot\tfrac14) + (\tfrac{13}{16}\cdot 1 - \tfrac12\cdot\tfrac58)\right| = 0 - \tfrac14 + \tfrac{3}{16} + \tfrac12 = \tfrac{7}{16}$.

Area $= \frac{7}{32}$ of the rectangle.

**Answer: (C) $\frac{7}{32}$**

kangaroo-at-2015-student-27.title: Halving triangles
kangaroo-at-2015-student-27.body:
Let the rectangle have width $w$, height $h$ and area $wh = 1$. Split the quadrilateral along the diagonal $M_1M_3$.
- Triangle $ABM_1$ has area $\frac12$. $M_2$ is the midpoint of $AM_1$, so $[M_1M_2B] = \frac12 [ABM_1] = \frac14$. $M_3$ is the midpoint of $BM_2$, so $[M_1M_2M_3] = \frac12[M_1M_2B] = \frac18$.
- $M_2$ is at height $\frac h2$, so $M_3$ (midpoint of $BM_2$) is at height $\frac h4$, i.e. at distance $\frac{3h}{4}$ from $DC$. Triangle $M_1M_3C$ has base $M_1C = \frac w2$ on $DC$, so its area is $\frac12\cdot\frac w2\cdot\frac{3h}{4} = \frac{3}{16}$. $M_4$ is the midpoint of $CM_3$, so $[M_1M_3M_4] = \frac12\cdot\frac{3}{16} = \frac{3}{32}$.

Total: $\frac18 + \frac{3}{32} = \frac{7}{32}$.

**Answer: (C) $\frac{7}{32}$**

kangaroo-at-2015-student-28.title: Set up equations
kangaroo-at-2015-student-28.body:
Squares are rectangles too. Let $r_s, b_s$ be the red/blue squares and $r_n, b_n$ the red/blue non-square rectangles.
- $r_s + b_s = 7$
- $r_s + r_n = b_s + 3$
- $r_s = b_s + b_n + 2$

From the first and third: $7 - b_s = b_s + b_n + 2$, so $b_n = 5 - 2b_s$. From the first two: $r_n = 2b_s - 4$. Both must be $\ge 0$: $b_s \ge 2$ and $b_s \le 2$, so $b_s = 2$, $b_n = 1$. Blue rectangles: $b_s + b_n = 3$.

**Answer: (B) 3**

kangaroo-at-2015-student-28.title: Check
kangaroo-at-2015-student-28.body:
With 2 blue squares, 1 blue non-square, 5 red squares and 0 red non-squares: squares $5 + 2 = 7$ ✓; red rectangles $5 = 2 + 3$ ✓; red squares $5 = 3 + 2$ ✓. So there are 3 blue rectangles.

**Answer: (B) 3**

kangaroo-at-2015-student-29.title: Josephus pattern
kangaroo-at-2015-student-29.body:
Every second person leaves. If the circle has a power of two, $2^k$, people and the count starts at person 1, then after one full round $2^{k-1}$ people remain and the count again starts at person 1 (the last person said an even number and left). So person 1 survives.

$96 = 64 + 32$. After 32 people have left (they said $2, 4, \dots, 64$), 64 people remain and the next one to count is the person who said 65 in round one. From now on this person plays the role of "person 1" in a circle of $64 = 2^6$, so he is the last one left.

**Answer: (D) 65**

kangaroo-at-2015-student-29.title: Round by round
kangaroo-at-2015-student-29.body:
Name each person by the number he said in round one. As long as a round has an even number of people, the first person of the round says an odd number, every second person leaves, and the last person of the round leaves, so the next round again starts with person 1 saying an odd number.
- Round 1 (96 people): $1, 3, 5, \dots, 95$ stay (48).
- Round 2: $1, 5, 9, \dots, 93$ stay (24).
- Round 3: $1, 9, 17, \dots, 89$ stay (12).
- Round 4: $1, 17, 33, 49, 65, 81$ stay (6).
- Round 5: $1, 33, 65$ stay (3); the next number, said by 1, is odd.
- Round 6: 1 stays (odd), 33 leaves (even), 65 stays (odd); then 1 says an even number and leaves.

Only person **65** is left.

**Answer: (D) 65**

kangaroo-at-2015-student-30.title: Divisibility rule for 11
kangaroo-at-2015-student-30.body:
KANGAROO has digits (from the left) $K, A, N, G, A, R, O, O$. A number is divisible by 11 iff the alternating sum of its digits is: $K - A + N - G + A - R + O - O = K + N - G - R \equiv 0 \pmod{11}$. The letters $A$ and $O$ cancel.

**Biggest:** make $K, A, N, G$ as big as possible in this order. $K = 9$, $A = 8$, $N = 7$; then $16 - G - R \equiv 0$, i.e. $G + R \equiv 16 \pmod{11}$, $G + R = 16$ or $5$. The biggest $G$ (from unused digits $0$–$6$) with a valid $R$: $G = 6$ needs $R = 10$ or $-1$ ✗; $G = 5$, $R = 0$ ✓. Then $O = 6$: $98758066$.

**Smallest:** $K = 1$, $A = 0$, $N = 2$; then $G + R \equiv 3$, so $G + R = 3$ or $14$. $G = 3$ needs $R = 0$ (taken) or $11$ ✗; $G = 4$: $R = 10$ ✗; $G = 5$, $R = 9$ ✓. Then $O = 3$: $10250933$.

In both numbers $G = 5$.

**Answer: (D) 5**

kangaroo-at-2015-student-30.title: Verify
kangaroo-at-2015-student-30.body:
Alternating digit sums: $9 - 8 + 7 - 5 + 8 - 0 + 6 - 6 = 11$ ✓. And $1 - 0 + 2 - 5 + 0 - 9 + 3 - 3 = -11$ ✓. Comparing letter by letter: K 9/1, A 8/0, N 7/2, G 5/5, R 0/9, O 6/3 — only G gets the same digit, 5.

**Answer: (D) 5**
